Will AI Throttle the Retirement Money Machine?
 
Plus, Big Tech’s election silver lining
 

Among the many winners in Wednesday’s postelection stock rally, big tech companies that are plowing money into data centers seemed out of place. But a forced slowdown in construction could be a reprieve from ruinous competition for them. The companies supplying the building boom aren’t faring as well. Stock futures are mixed and oil prices have stabilized at a much lower level now that the blue wave dust has begun to clear.

Thank you for your contribution

 

We’ve all heard that the AI boom needs a lot of resources—power, water, chips, copper, land.

 

But money is what makes the world go round. White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett reassured nervous investors this week that there’s no shortage of capital for the AI build-out. 

 

At what price, though? A slowdown of cash going into stock funds could dent lofty valuations and raise problems for the industry as thorny as this week’s blue wave.

 

A report published late last month lays out a scenario in which AI undermines a key source of capital—retirement savings. Duncan Lamont, head of strategic research at Schroders, says that we focus too much on short-term indicators of market health and need to consider that flow. Most comes from automatic paycheck withdrawals invested blindly.

 

“These contributions don’t care about valuations, they don’t care about headlines, they don’t care about midterms” says Lamont.

 

If AI really takes hold in the economy then it could mean job losses. Schroders sees unemployment hitting 10% by 2030 in a boom scenario. Anthropic boss Dario Amodei told The Wall Street Journal that the future could see 5% to 10% economic growth but 10% unemployment. 

 

Those are scary numbers, but even a milder job shock would hit the people who make the lion’s share of retirement contributions. About 87% and 80% of finance and tech workers, respectively, participate in workplace plans. They also have the highest salaries and company matches.

 

Groups typically hit harder during recessions might be safer in an AI jobspocalypse. They’re also far less likely to contribute to 401(k) plans. Only 14% of leisure and hospitality workers do and they earn a lot less on average than people in those more-exposed professions.

 

The good news is that widespread AI-related layoffs haven’t happened yet. What that statistic misses, though, is a lot less hiring of young people in white-collar roles such as software development since ChatGPT launched.

 

They earn less than their older colleagues, but still more than most Americans. And Lamont points out that young professionals tend to allocate a larger share of their retirement contributions to stocks than late-career savers nearing retirement.

 

Including all sources such as stock buybacks. Lamont says recent years have seen close to half a trillion annually flow from defined-contribution plans and individual retirement accounts into U.S. stocks alone. That has fluctuated between 30 cents and 78 cents for every other dollar of net demand for stocks.

 

In other words, it’s a lot. And a modest change in buying at the margin can have a big effect on stocks. More price-sensitive investors might be less enthusiastic about valuing loss-making AI companies at $1.5 trillion, for example.

↘️Zillow: The company reported a drop in traffic to its apps and sites in the midst of what it called “one of the toughest housing markets in a generation.” The stock fell about 15% premarket.

 

↘️ SoftBank and ABB: China blocked SoftBank’s $5.4 billion acquisition of Swedish firm ABB’s robotics unit, highlighting Beijing’s determination to lock in its AI edge. SoftBank fell nearly 7% (post-U.S. midterms concerns about the AI trade also weighed on the stock), while ABB shares slipped.

 

↘️Arm: Shares slipped about 3% premarket even as the chip company reported a 27% jump in revenue in its latest quarter.

 

↗️Toyota Motor: The Japanese automaker’s stock soared after it lifted its earnings forecast, with a weaker yen and cost cuts boosting profitability.
